proposal.utterance: Classify 'Abusus' (the right of abuse, in Roman-law property theory) in BFO terms.

entities.label: Abusus
entities.rationale: Abusus is the Roman-law entitlement to alienate, consume, or destroy a thing—one of the three classic jura (usus, fructus, abusus) constituting dominium. It is externally grounded: it is conferred on a person by a legal system's recognition of ownership and can be present or absent depending on legal status (e.g., a usufructuary lacks abusus). This external, socially/legally-conferred grounding makes it a Role (BFO_0000023) rather than a Disposition. It is a kind (class), not a named individual, since many property-holders throughout Roman and civil-law history bear an instance of Abusus. Placing it as a subclass of LegalRight captures that it is a species of legally-conferred entitlement.

relations.rationale: Abusus is a specific species of LegalRight (itself typed as BFO_0000023 Role): it is the particular legal entitlement of alienation/consumption/destruction that inheres in the owner-role of a res within a Roman or civil-law property system.
Reinforces that Abusus is a Role: externally grounded, inhering in a bearer (the owner), dependent on the legal system's recognition, and realizable in acts of alienation or consumption.

open_questions: Should Abusus be further distinguished from its co-constituents of dominium (Usus, Fructus)? Modelling the mereological relationship among these three as parts of a composite LegalRight (dominium) may be warranted—shall we mint Usus and Fructus as sibling classes now?

Is the intended scope classical Roman law only, or should the class also cover derivative civil-law systems (French Code Civil Art. 544, etc.)? This may affect whether Abusus is defined narrowly under a 'RomanLawRight' subhierarchy.

Should we model the bearer of an Abusus instance as a 'Dominus' (owner) Role on a person, linked via RO_0000057 (has participant) to an act of alienation (BFO_0000015)? That would let us represent the realization of Abusus in concrete transactions.

Is there a need to distinguish the jus abusendi as a normative power (Hohfeldian power to transfer title) from a liberty (permission to destroy)? This might require introducing a 'LegalPower' subclass of Role alongside LegalRight.
proposal.rationale_summary: Abusus, the Roman-law right to alienate or destroy a thing (jus abutendi), is most accurately typed in BFO as a Role (BFO_0000023): it is a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in a property-owner (the bearer) and is externally grounded in the legal system's recognition of dominium rather than in any intrinsic physical feature of the owner or the res. Because many past and present owners each bear their own instance of Abusus, it is appropriately modelled as a class rather than an individual. Placing it as a subclass of the existing working:LegalRight class (itself a subclass of BFO_0000023) preserves the existing hierarchy while adding the specificity of the abusus facet of ownership. The role is realizable in processes of alienation, consumption, or destruction (BFO_0000015), but we do not assert those realization relations here pending user confirmation of scope and sibling concepts.
